title: Food webs & network ecology
sub: Symposium topic 4 · Paine 1966 vs Bartley et al. 2019
blurb: Keystone species, interaction strength, network structure and rewiring, with Lake Nakuru as the example.
lede: Group 4's question: does food-web complexity build local biodiversity? Their example ecosystem was Lake Nakuru in Kenya. Classic: Paine (1966), food web complexity and species diversity. Recent: Bartley et al. (2019), food web rewiring in a changing world.
six: **Keystone species**: a disproportionately large effect relative to its biomass; removing it can trigger cascades or regime shifts.
**Interaction strength**: how strongly one species affects another's vital rates, abundance or behaviour.
**Network structure**: degree (number of links; hubs), modularity (clusters), motifs (recurring small patterns).
**Network rewiring**: who interacts with whom changes over time, from seasons and range shifts or from humans (land use, invasions, climate).
Complexity (many links, alternative prey, varied niches) supports **resilience**, but complex webs are **not automatically stable**.
Lake Nakuru: cyanobacteria (Spirulina/Arthrospira) → lesser flamingo and soda tilapia → pelicans, cormorants, fish eagle.
foot: Source: Group 4 symposium slides; glossary section 5.

questions.q: A keystone species is one that…
questions.answer: Has a disproportionately large effect relative to its biomass or abundance
wrong: Is the largest predator by body size
questions.e: Glossary 5a: removing it can cause big shifts, cascades or regime shifts.

questions.answer: How strongly one species affects another's vital rates, abundance or behaviour
wrong: How many species live in a web
How long a food chain is
questions.e: E.g. per-capita effect of a predator on prey mortality.

questions.q: In a network, a species' degree is…
questions.answer: The number of links it has

questions.q: Modularity in a food web means…
questions.answer: Clusters of species interact more within than between clusters
wrong: The web has only one chain

questions.q: Small link patterns that recur more often than chance are called…

questions.answer: A change over time in who interacts with whom
wrong: Moving species to new places on purpose
Adding fences to keep predators out
questions.e: Links weaken, disappear or form; drivers can be natural or human.

questions.q: Which is a human driver of rewiring named in the glossary?
questions.e: Human drivers: land-use change, species introductions, climate change.

questions.q: How do invasive species rewire food webs, according to Group 4?
questions.answer: Through resource competition, direct predation, indirect effects and network disruption
wrong: Only by adding food for natives
By making webs simpler and always more stable
They have no effect on links
questions.e: Invaders change links across several trophic levels.

questions.q: What did Group 4 conclude about complexity and stability?
questions.answer: Complexity supports resilience, but highly complex webs are not automatically stable
wrong: Simple webs are always more diverse
questions.e: Multiple feeding links and alternative prey routes help.

questions.q: At Lake Nakuru, what does the lesser flamingo feed on?
questions.e: A specialised filter feeder and the dominant consumer by biomass.

questions.q: At Lake Nakuru, the great white pelican mainly eats…
Why do alternative prey routes help a food web?
questions.answer: Diet switching keeps energy flowing when one prey declines

vocab.meaning: A species with a much bigger effect on community or ecosystem than its biomass suggests.
A high-degree species with many links.
How strongly one species affects another's vital rates, abundance or behaviour.
Number of links a species has in the web.
Clusters of species that interact more within than between clusters.
Small link pattern that recurs more often than by chance.
Change over time in who interacts with whom.
Ability of a web to keep functioning when species decline.
Animal that sieves small food items from water (lesser flamingo).

facts: The number of links a species has is its {degree|motif|module|level}.
Removing a {keystone|dominant|introduced|rare} species can trigger large community shifts.
Changes over time in who eats whom are called network {rewiring|modularity|degree|cascades}.
Highly complex webs are not automatically {stable|diverse|large|connected}.
